proof:
Source. Step 2 of the supplied proof of the parent ("Fix an orthonormal basis a_0, …, a_m of A₀ and let Ω(v_0, …, v_m) := det(a_i·v_j)_{i,j=0..m}, an alternating (m+1)-linear form on ℝ^P. Ω(v_0, …, v_m) = 0 if the v_j are linearly dependent or if some v_j is orthogonal to A₀; Ω(w_0, …, w_m) = ±1 for every orthonormal basis (w_j) of A₀ (the matrix (a_i·w_j) is orthogonal); Ω ≠ 0 on every basis of A₀"), together with the A₀-representative Σ_i Ω(…, a_i)a_i of the functional v ↦ Ω(…, v) used in its steps 3 and 5. The free vector slot of Ω is placed first here instead of last; this changes Ω(…) only by the sign (−1)^m, which is irrelevant for (i)–(iv).
Notation: the slots of Ω are indexed by 0, …, m; for u ∈ ℝ^P and w = (w_1, …, w_m) write (u, w) := (u, w_1, …, w_m) (Fin.cons u w). P_{A₀} denotes the orthogonal projection onto A₀.

1. (The volume form Ω.) Fix an orthonormal basis a_0, …, a_m of A₀ (it exists because dim A₀ = m + 1) and put Ω(v) := det(a_i·v_j)_{i,j=0..m} for v = (v_0, …, v_m) ∈ (ℝ^P)^{m+1}. Column j of the matrix depends linearly on v_j, so Ω is (m+1)-linear; if v_j = v_k for some j ≠ k, two columns coincide and Ω(v) = 0, so Ω is alternating. Since a_i·v_j = a_i·P_{A₀}(v_j), Ω(v) is unchanged if any v_j is replaced by P_{A₀}(v_j).

2. (Definition of N.) For w ∈ (ℝ^P)^m put N(w) := Σ_{i=0}^m Ω(a_i, w) a_i. For each fixed i, w ↦ Ω(a_i, w) is m-linear and alternating (step 1), so N is an alternating m-linear map ℝ^P × ⋯ × ℝ^P → ℝ^P. N is continuous: Ω(a_i, w) is the determinant of an (m+1)×(m+1) matrix whose entries a_k·a_i and a_k·w_j depend continuously (linearly) on w, and the determinant is a polynomial in the entries (Mathlib Continuous.matrix_det); so N is a continuous alternating map, i.e. N ∈ Euclid P [⋀^Fin m]→L[ℝ] Euclid P.

3. (Key identity.) For every u ∈ ℝ^P, N(w)·u = Ω(u, w). Indeed N(w)·u = Σ_i Ω(a_i, w)(a_i·u) = Ω(Σ_i (a_i·u)a_i, w) by linearity of Ω in slot 0, and Σ_i (a_i·u)a_i = P_{A₀}(u), so by step 1 this equals Ω(P_{A₀}(u), w) = Ω(u, w).

4. (i) N(w) is a linear combination of a_0, …, a_m ∈ A₀, hence N(w) ∈ A₀.

5. (ii) For j ∈ {1, …, m}, step 3 gives N(w)·w_j = Ω(w_j, w_1, …, w_m). The vector w_j occupies slot 0 and slot j, so this is 0 because Ω is alternating.

6. (The normal line of span w in A₀.) Suppose every w_j lies in A₀ and (w_1, …, w_m) is linearly independent; let S := span{w_1, …, w_m} ⊆ A₀, so dim S = m. The orthogonal complement of S inside A₀, A₀ ∩ S^⊥, has dimension (m + 1) − m = 1; let e be a unit vector in it. By (i), (ii) and linearity, N(w) ∈ A₀ and N(w) ⊥ S, so N(w) ∈ A₀ ∩ S^⊥ = ℝe, and N(w) = (N(w)·e)e = Ω(e, w)e by step 3. The family (e, w_1, …, w_m) is linearly independent (e ≠ 0 and e ⊥ S) and consists of m + 1 vectors of the (m+1)-dimensional space A₀, so it is a basis of A₀.

7. (iv) In the situation of step 6 let C := (a_i·(e, w)_j)_{i,j=0..m}. Every b ∈ A₀ equals Σ_i (a_i·b)a_i, so the columns of C are the coordinate vectors of the basis (e, w) of A₀ with respect to the basis (a_i); hence C is invertible and Ω(e, w) = det C ≠ 0. Therefore N(w) = Ω(e, w)e ≠ 0.

8. (iii) If (w_j) is orthonormal and every w_j ∈ A₀, it is linearly independent, so step 6 applies, and now (e, w_1, …, w_m) is an orthonormal basis of A₀. For b, b' ∈ A₀, Parseval's identity in the orthonormal basis (a_i) gives b·b' = Σ_i (a_i·b)(a_i·b'); so the columns of C are orthonormal in ℝ^{m+1}, CᵀC = I and det C = ±1. Hence |N(w)| = |Ω(e, w)|·|e| = |det C| = 1. ∎
key_steps: Ω(v_0, …, v_m) := det(a_i·v_j) for an orthonormal basis (a_i) of A₀ is alternating and sees only the A₀-components of its arguments.
N(w) := Σ_i Ω(a_i, w)a_i is a continuous alternating map with N(w)·u = Ω(u, w) for all u.
Hence N(w) ∈ A₀ and N(w)·w_j = Ω(w_j, w) = 0 (repeated argument).
For independent w in A₀, N(w) = Ω(e, w)e with e the unit normal of span w in A₀; Ω(e, w) is the determinant of a change of basis, nonzero, and ±1 when w is orthonormal.
